content: Scientists expected Zimbabwe’s fossil beds to yield familiar South African dinosaurs, but the newly named Musango is helping reveal a distinct prehistoric community. Africa boasts up to 25% of Earth’s animal and plant species . This diversity is driven by diverse habitats: harsh deserts, vast grasslands, dense forests, towering mountains, lush coastlines, and teeming seas. It is also due to deep evolutionary roots, as many animal and plant groups originated here in the distant past. Paleontologists have been excavating this material for nearly two centuries . Africa is most famous for spectacular hominid fossils that reveal our own ancestry. However, the continent boasts many fabulous fossil finds, including those of the most familiar extinct animals – dinosaurs. The first African dinosaur fossils to be noted scientifically hailed from the Eastern Cape, South Africa, and were described in the 1850s. Since then, the African dinosaur map has expanded, with rich fossil beds in South Africa, Lesotho, Tanzania, Egypt, Niger, Malawi, Madagascar, and Morocco. Zimbabwe is an important part of the African dinosaur puzzle, with dinosaur bones reported since 1916 . As a specialist on early dinosaurs who has worked on similar material from China, the UK and Africa, I’ve been drawn to these Zimbabwean fossils to see what they reveal about the first stages of their evolution. Our latest addition to the Triassic zoo, Musango matusadonaensis , is a sauropodomorph dinosaur. (That’s the dinosaur subgroup that eventually gave rise to four-legged, long-necked giants like Diplodocus .) Its incomplete skeleton was found in the bank of the Nyamasango River close to Musango Island, as captured in the animal’s scientific name. Musango ’s anatomy shows us that it was bipedal (walking on its hind legs only), reached about 4.5 meters in length, and weighed 220 kg. Growth marks in its bones reveal that it was a subadult when it died. Sadly, the skull wasn’t preserved, so its diet is unknown, but its close relatives were largely herbivorous (plant-eating). Our new work reveals something unexpected about Zimbabwean dinosaurs. They’re not simply an extension of better-known South African faunas but include an array of species unique to the region. We’re now trying to work out why these differences exist. We suspect that environmental conditions might be the key. Early fossil finds in Zimbabwe were overlooked by many scientists, and it was not until the 1970s that they became more generally known . This was thanks to pioneering work by Zimbabwean paleontologists Geoffrey Bond and Michael Raath, who discovered abundant material in the hinterlands of Bulawayo (south-west Zimbabwe) and the lower Zambezi Valley (forming the border with Zambia). Most of these finds were identified as belonging to known species named from neighboring South Africa. Palaeontological work in Zimbabwe stalled for a few decades. However, a band of devoted fossil hunters kept searching. One of them, Steve Edwards, a local safari camp manager, found new, productive sites on the shore of Lake Kariba, the artificial lake which forms most of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. News of the discoveries eventually reached Jonah Choiniere at the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg. Jonah, an expert on early dinosaurs, immediately recognized the importance of the material. He assembled an international team of South African, Zimbabwean, and UK-based collaborators to explore them further. This was a major task, as the sites on Late Kariba’s shoreline are deep inside Matusadona National Park. Our solution was to use one of the Kariba houseboats as a mobile hotel and laboratory, so that we could prospect the shoreline. We mounted two expeditions, in 2017 and 2018. We have been cleaning and studying this material ever since. Both trips yielded a trove of material, collected from brick-red mudstones and sandstones that were laid down by ancient rivers around 210 million years ago, during the Late Triassic period (237-201 million years ago) . Geological evidence and plant fossils show that the Triassic landscape of Kariba was dry and dotted with stands of large conifer trees, with green corridors of vegetation following permanent watercourses. Sauropodomorphs are the most common Late Triassic dinosaurs. But what’s interesting about Musango and its relative Musankwa (which we described from the same beds in 2024) is that they are unique to Zimbabwe. We’d expected to find South African dinosaur species in these beds, given their similar age and geographic proximity, but surprisingly all the material we’ve collected so far has revealed animals that are distinct from those elsewhere. These Zimbabwean dinosaurs are not even the closest relatives of their South African neighbors. We’ve also found other fossil animals, including lungfish and aquatic reptiles called phytosaurs, which are rare or absent in South African sites. Following this, we’ve started to reappraise the historical dinosaur collections in Bulawayo. It appears that many of these fossils can’t be referred to South African species either, contrary to earlier assumptions. Then, as now, Zimbabwe was further north than South Africa and closer to the equator, so climatic differences might be responsible for these varied casts of characters (as climate is known to have a strong effect on the distributions of living animals). To probe this further, we’ll be going back to Kariba in search of more fossils. We’ll also collect more information on the exact ages and environments of these dinosaur-bearing rocks, to compare them more precisely with sites elsewhere. Although the significance of these dinosaurs is only just coming to light, Zimbabwe is already taking a greater role in shedding much-needed light on early dinosaur evolution. title: OpenAI Saudi national bugging case shows threat to U.S. leadership in AI: DNI Clayton
content: U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday. AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on " Squawk Box ." It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force . Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications. Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors. "The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said. "It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said. The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said. An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg." Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding." The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said. The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race. "We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

Climate change could give African antelopes an edge in the American West, with native wildlife facing tougher competition when drought leaves less to eat. An antelope native to southern Africa’s Kalahari Desert has found a foothold in New Mexico’s dry rangelands, and climate change could give it far more of the American West to roam. Gemsbok were brought to the state for hunting in the 1960s and 1970s and have since spread more than 100 kilometers, or about 62 miles, from their release point. A new study by researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign suggests that suitable habitat could expand well beyond New Mexico by 2100, reaching into Texas, Arizona, Utah, California, and even southern Washington and Montana. The same adaptations that help gemsbok survive in arid country could give them an advantage over native wildlife as those conditions become more widespread, raising concerns about the animals and grasslands that would have to support growing herds. “Gemsbok are famous for being really well adapted to heat and drought. In addition to other heat adaptations, they can get all of their water from plants, so they don’t really need to drink. That’s really unusual for animals that big — they can weigh 450 pounds. They’re the poster species for dealing with the kind of changes we’re going to see in the Southwest,” said study co-author Bob Schooley, professor and head of the university’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences, or NRES. The researchers built their forecasts around the places gemsbok already inhabit. For each recorded location, they examined precipitation, temperature seasonality, vegetation cover, terrain ruggedness, and human population density to identify the combination of conditions associated with the animals’ presence. People sharing wildlife photographs online supplied the sightings that made this analysis possible. “We turned towards participant science to do this work. When people contribute photos to apps like iNaturalist, the occurrence records get scraped into something called the Global Biodiversity Information Facility. From that, we were able to use a statistical method called Maxent to find habitat associations for gemsbok,” said lead author Nathan Alexander. He began the research as a doctoral student in NRES, part of the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences at Illinois, and is now a postdoctoral scholar at Southern Illinois University. Using those habitat associations, the team searched for similar environments elsewhere and projected where they could occur under future climate scenarios. The resulting maps suggest that gemsbok could gain more than additional land to occupy. Areas that are currently separated could become connected, potentially making it easier for the animals to move between them. “When there are these isolated patches, there might be dispersal barriers that they can’t cross to get to the next patch. But when these patches coalesce and connect, there might be increased opportunities for gemsbok to invade and expand into these novel habitats. We see this particularly in western Texas, but also into western New Mexico and up into Arizona, and even some regions of California, like Death Valley,” said Kieran Andreoni. He began the research as a master’s student in NRES and is now conservation director at the Southern Plains Land Trust in Colorado. Gemsbok would still have to reach that territory and establish populations for the projected habitat expansion to translate into a wider occupied range. If they do, larger herds could consume more of the forage that cattle and native grazers such as pronghorn and bison depend on, leaving less food to go around. “Along with that diet overlap, gemsbok are able to forage on lower quality plant materials than some of our native species,” Alexander said. “So in drought years, we could imagine our native species might be a little bit more stressed and nutrient deficient, whereas the gemsbok are going to be able to move to less nutrient-rich plant material and still be able to persist in the environment.” Gemsbok also left their natural predators, lions and hyenas, behind in Africa. Coyotes and mountain lions in the Southwest kill far fewer of the antelopes, according to Schooley. With relatively little pressure from predators and the ability to keep feeding as forage quality declines, growing herds could continue grazing land that is already struggling through drought. “These desert rangelands are often used for cattle grazing. When there’s a severe drought, they pull the cattle off the landscape because there’s no food for them. Well, no one pulls the gemsbok off. Considering their ability to survive on low-quality forage, they could severely damage remaining grasslands. So I think that’s the kind of thing we worry about — what are the implications when they get to even larger numbers?” Schooley said. Gemsbok in the Southwest have also tested positive for malignant catarrhal fever, bovine respiratory syncytial virus, and bovine para-influenza-3, all of concern to the cattle industry. Alexander said the antelopes could carry and spread diseases to domestic and native ungulates, or hoofed mammals, adding a potential disease risk to the competition for food. Conservationists, ranchers, and hunting operations bring competing interests to decisions about gemsbok, making future population management difficult but critical, the researchers say. On New Mexico’s dry rangelands, and potentially far beyond them, keeping herds in check could help protect the food that cattle and native wildlife need when drought leaves less to share. Reference: “Predicted range expansion of exotic Gemsbok (Oryx gazella) under climate change in the United States” by Nathan Alexander, Kieran J Andreoni and Robert L Schooley, 26 September 2026, Journal of Mammalogy .
